Light House

GeometryCurvesCircles
Game: Watch the shape made where the beams from two turning lighthouses cross.
How to play: Drag the three points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Choose the number of beams and each speed, then press Go to watch them sweep.
Look for the math

The old cut-the-knot page still serves its Java applet notice, so the picture here is rebuilt from the page's text and the applet's own bytecode. The surprise is that beams spinning at completely different speeds still meet in the corners of a perfectly regular polygon.

The lighthouse theorem

The page claims that if each lighthouse sends out beams equally spaced through 360°, the pairwise crossings form regular polygons: regular triangles for three beams, squares for four beams, and so on. The logic test checks this exhaustively for every beam count the applet allows (1 to 12), every pair of speeds from −12 to 12, every one of the N polygons, and five different times: the N crossings always have equal sides, equal turns of 360/N degrees, and lie on one circle. The claim is true; the size and position of the polygon change, never its regularity.

Why half a step matters

A beam is a whole line through its lighthouse, so N distinct lines are spaced π/N apart. Take beam j of the first fan at angle a + jπ/N and beam j of the second fan at b + (j+i+1)π/N. The extra π/N is half a step: the second fan is staggered halfway between the first one's beams. This is the same angle-chasing idea behind inscribed angles in a circle. The index i just turns the whole polygon by another step, giving N different polygons at once.

The speeds only change the size

Each beam turns with a constant angular velocity. The applet adds π/Ngon × Rate to a beam's angle at every animation step, where the bucket Ngon is chosen from the average distance of the three draggable points from their circumcentre. One fan may even stand still (speed 0) or spin the other way (negative speed): the crossings still make a regular N-gon, sometimes very large, because every angle in the fan moves by the same amount each tick.

Where the original differs

The applet's own ComputeSignedAngle signs its angle opposite to the (cos, -sin) direction that GetNext uses. Its Shift then mirrors a beam at every step, so the Java picture repeats crossings instead of drawing N different ones. That is a bug in the implementation, not in the theorem the page states, so this port follows the page: its fans really are spaced evenly and its N crossings really are distinct. The check script keeps a literal transcription of the Java array to pin down exactly where the two differ.

Try three beams with speeds 2 and −1, press Go, and watch a triangle sweep past; then set speed 1 to 0 and see the triangle keep its shape while only its size changes.
